stages.name: Government intervention: tax incidence and its drawbacks
stages.title: Tax incidence and its drawbacks
stages.sub: After this the student can explain who really bears a tax and why that creates problems for government policy.

steps.q: A £1 tax is put on cigarettes, where demand barely falls when price rises. The seller puts the price up by 90p. Who ends up paying most of that £1?
steps.hint: Think about how much of the price rise the buyer actually accepted, since they kept buying anyway.

steps.q: Now compare two goods: one where buyers barely react to a price rise, one where they react a lot. In which case can sellers pass on more of the tax to buyers?
steps.right: The good where buyers barely react
steps.wrong: The good where buyers react a lot
steps.hint: If buyers keep buying despite the price rise, how much of the extra cost can the seller shift onto them?

steps.q: Cigarette tax is passed on mostly to buyers. A pensioner on a low income and a wealthy banker both smoke the same amount. Does the tax take a bigger slice of income from one of them?
steps.right: Yes, a bigger slice from the pensioner's income
steps.wrong: No, it takes the same slice from both
steps.hint: They pay the same extra pounds, but their incomes are very different sizes.
